hook.line: Vale's mother wants to know everything about the café and the people in it. You already have my, your and his. To talk about the café as a team, you need our.
hook.es: Mamá, nuestro café es pequeño, pero nuestros clientes son muy simpáticos.
hook.en: Mum, our café is small, but our customers are really nice.

examples.es: Vale y su hermana hablan por teléfono.
examples.en: Vale and her sister are talking on the phone.
Do your parents live in Toronto? (to a friend)

rule:
You know *mi*, *tu* and *su*, plus an *s* for more than one thing: *mis amigos*.

The new one is our, and it has four forms, because it matches the thing like an adjective does:
*nuestro café*
*nuestra abuela*
*nuestros clientes*
*nuestras mesas*

It follows the thing, never the owners. Tomás and Vale are two people, but it's one café: *nuestro café*.

Now the busy one. *Su* means his, her, its, their, your (formal) and your (you all). *Su novio* can be her boyfriend or your boyfriend if you speak to someone formally. The conversation almost always decides. When it doesn't, use the name: *el novio de Vale*.

English has one word per owner. Spanish has fewer words, so each one carries more.
smallPrint: Teachers call these possessive determiners (*posesivos*). *Nuestro* is the only one that changes for masculine and feminine.

options: Your house is small. (to a friend)
Your eyes are dark. (to a friend)
Your girlfriend is really nice. (to a friend)
Your brother is tall. (to a friend)
Your brothers are tall. (to a friend)
Your aunt has blond hair. (to a friend)

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: ___ abuela es de Bogotá. (Nuestro / Nuestra) Our grandmother.
yourTurn.why: *Abuela* is feminine, so our takes the *a*: *nuestra*.

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: ___ clientes son simpáticos. (Nuestro / Nuestros) Our customers.

accept: Mis hermanas tienen el pelo negro.
yourTurn.why: More than one sister, so *mis*, and *morenas* matches them.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask Don Hernando, politely: Is this your coffee?
Make it about our: Mi casa es pequeña.
Make it plural: Nuestra mesa es vieja.
Make it about Vale: Mi hermana vive en Medellín. (Her sister lives in Medellín.)

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Nuestro* matches the thing, and *abuela* is feminine: *nuestra*.
Close. Two owners, but one café: no *s*.

pitfalls.wrong: Vale y la su hermana hablan.
pitfalls.why: *Su* already does the job of *la*. Never use both.

personal: Think of a group you belong to: your family, your team, your flatmates. Write three lines about something that is yours together, using *nuestro*, *nuestra*, *nuestros* or *nuestras*.
